title: Probe cycles — start here
body:
## What the probe is
The probe is a tool that goes in the spindle like any other, except it does not cut.
It has a stylus with a ruby ball on the end. When that ball touches the part, the machine
stops and records exactly where it was. That is all it does: it tells the machine where
metal is.

On this machine the probe is **tool #60**.

## What these cycles are for
You put a part in the vise or fixture. The machine does not know where it is. You have to
tell it. That is the work offset — the machine's idea of where zero is on your part.

These cycles find it for you. The probe touches the part a few times, works out the real
position, and writes it straight into the work offset. No edge finder, no indicator, no
math on paper.

## How a cycle is written
Every cycle is the same macro call. The **A** number picks which cycle you want, then you
add whatever that cycle needs, then M30 ends the program.

`G65 P9023 A1. D1. S57.`

Read that as: run cycle A1, the hole is about 1 inch, write the answer into offset 57.

Notice every number has a **decimal point**. Leave it off and the control reads the value
wrong.

## S — which work offset to write into
- `S54.` through `S59.` writes to **G54 through G59**
- `S101.` through `S148.` writes to **G54.1 P1 through G54.1 P48**

So `S57.` means G57. Pick the offset your program actually uses, or you will set up the
wrong one and not find out until the tool is in the cut.

## The other letters
- **D** — about how big the hole or boss is
- **X** or **Y** — about how wide the slot or web is
- **Z** — how far down to move, written as a negative number
- **B** — angle shift, only on the 3-point cycles

"About how big" means roughly. The probe needs a starting guess so it knows how far to
reach before it expects to touch something. A rough number is fine. A badly wrong number
means it either stops short and alarms out, or keeps going and breaks the stylus.

## Before you press cycle start
1. Put the probe in the spindle.
2. Jog it so the ball is sitting near the middle of the feature, above it.
3. Check the numbers in the program match the part in front of you. The saved programs
   have leftover example values in them.
4. First time on a new setup, hand on the feed hold.

## The full list
- **A1** inner diameter — O7001
- **A2** outer diameter — O7002
- **A3** slot center — O7003
- **A4** web center — O7004
- **A5** X+ edge — O7005
- **A6** X- edge — O7006
- **A7** Y+ edge — O7007
- **A8** Y- edge — O7008
- **A9** Z find — O7009
- **A11** 3-point inner diameter — O7011
- **A12** 3-point outer diameter — O7012
- **A14** A-axis align — O7014
- **A15** C-axis align at A-90 — O7015
- **A16** C-axis align along X — O7016
- **A17** C-axis align along Y — O7017

A10 and A13 are not in our saved programs. They may exist on the control — nobody has
checked.

title: Probe: center of a hole or a round boss
body:
Use these when the thing you are picking up is **round** — a bored hole, or a round post
sticking up. The probe touches it in several spots, works out the true center, and writes
that center into the work offset.

## A1 — inside a hole
The probe starts inside the hole and reaches outward until it touches the wall.

`G65 P9023 A1. D1. S57.`

**D** is roughly how big the hole is across. `D1.` means about one inch.

## A2 — outside a round boss
The probe has to drop down beside the post first, then reach in toward it. That is what
the Z is for.

`G65 P9023 A2. D4. Z-0.7 S57.`

**D** is roughly the diameter of the boss. **Z-0.7** means drop seven tenths below where
the probe is sitting now, so the ball ends up alongside the post instead of over the top
of it.

Z is **incremental** — it moves that far from wherever the probe is right now, not to a
fixed height. Start too high and it will reach in above the part and touch nothing.

## A11 and A12 — the 3-point versions
Same job, but the probe takes three touches instead of four, and **B** lets you rotate
where those touches land.

`G65 P9023 A11. B45. D1. S57.`    inside a hole

`G65 P9023 A12. B45. D4. Z-0.7 S57.`    outside a boss

Use these when something is in the way of a normal pickup — a keyway, a slot cutting
through the bore, a gap in the boss. Set **B** so the touches miss the interruption.
`B45.` shifts them 45 degrees around.

## Watch out
- If the hole has a keyway and you run plain A1, the probe may drop into the slot and give
  you a center that is off. Use A11 and shift the angle.
- On A2 and A12, make sure the Z drop clears the top of the part but stays on the boss. Too
  far down and you are probing the shoulder, not the post.

title: Probe: center of a slot or a web
body:
Same idea as a hole or boss, but for straight-sided features. The probe touches both
sides and puts zero exactly in the middle.

A **slot** is a channel cut into the part — the probe sits inside it and reaches out.
A **web** is a rib or rail standing up — the probe goes down beside it and reaches in.

## A3 — inside a slot
`G65 P9023 A3. Y1. S57.`

Give it **X** or **Y**, whichever way the slot runs across. The example says `Y1.` — about
one inch wide, measured in Y. If the slot runs the other way, use X instead.

## A4 — across a web
`G65 P9023 A4. X4. Z-0.7 S57.`

Same deal, plus **Z** because the probe has to get down beside the rib before it can reach
in. `Z-0.7` drops seven tenths from where it sits now.

## Pick X or Y, not both
You are telling it which direction to measure in. If the slot runs left to right, that is
X. Front to back is Y. Only give it the one.

## Watch out
- This finds the center in one direction only. A slot pickup gives you the middle across
  the slot, not along it.
- On A4, if the Z drop does not clear the top of the web, the probe reaches in over the top
  and touches nothing.

title: Probe: an edge or the top of the part
body:
The simplest ones. One touch, one face, one number into the offset. These replace an edge
finder.

## The four edges
The letter in the name is the direction the probe **travels** to go find the face.

- **A5** — moves in X+ (to the right) until it touches
- **A6** — moves in X- (to the left)
- **A7** — moves in Y+ (away from you)
- **A8** — moves in Y- (toward you)

`G65 P9023 A5. S57.`

`G65 P9023 A6. S57.`

`G65 P9023 A7. S57.`

`G65 P9023 A8. S57.`

No size argument on any of them. The only thing you tell it is which offset to write into.

## Which one do I want
Stand where you are and look at the part. Ask which way the probe has to move to reach the
face you care about. That is your cycle.

Probe is to the left of the part and you want that left face: the probe moves right to get
there, so **A5**.

## A9 — top of the part
`G65 P9023 A9. S57.`

Touches straight down and sets Z zero on the surface the ball lands on. Jog over the spot
you want zero on first, because it sets it wherever it happens to be.

## Watch out
- Position the probe close to the face before you start. These reach a set distance and
  alarm out if they find nothing.
- Get the direction wrong and the probe drives away from the part, finds nothing, and
  alarms. Annoying but harmless. Getting it wrong toward a fixture is the expensive one.
- A9 sets Z on whatever is under the ball. Over a hole, over a chip, over the vise jaw —
  it does not know the difference.

title: Probe: squaring up a part (A and C axis align)
body:
These are for when the part is not sitting square. Instead of tapping it straight with a
mallet, the probe touches a face in two places, works out how far off it is, and corrects
for it in the work offset.

Saves a lot of time on a 5-axis setup where getting a part physically square is a pain.

## How they are written
Each one takes two numbers:

- the **first** is how far apart the two touch points are along the face
- the **second** is how far the probe moves in to make contact, written negative or small

## A14 — A-axis align
`G65 P9023 A14. Y1.25 Z-0.5 S57.`

**Y1.25** — touch two points an inch and a quarter apart along Y.
**Z-0.5** — drop half an inch to reach the face.

## A15 — C-axis align with the table tipped to A-90
`G65 P9023 A15. X1.25 Z-0.5 S57.`

**X1.25** — two points an inch and a quarter apart along X.
**Z-0.5** — drop half an inch in.

Only for when the A axis is already at -90.

## A16 — C-axis align, face running along X
`G65 P9023 A16. X7. Y0.5 S1.`

**X7.** — two points seven inches apart along X. Further apart reads more accurately.
**Y0.5** — move half an inch in Y to touch.

## A17 — C-axis align, face running along Y
`G65 P9023 A17. Y6.5 X0.5 S54.`

**Y6.5** — two points six and a half inches apart along Y.
**X0.5** — move half an inch in X to touch.

## A16 or A17, which one
Look at the face you are indicating off. If it runs left to right, that is along X, so
**A16**. If it runs front to back, that is along Y, so **A17**.

## Watch out
- **The saved O7016 has `S1.` in it.** That is not a valid offset — the list only goes
  `S54.` to `S59.` and `S101.` to `S148.` Looks like a typo. Change it before running.
- Spread the two touch points as far apart as the face allows. Close together and a small
  measuring error turns into a big angle error.
- Both points have to land on the same flat face. A chamfer or a burr under one of them
  throws the whole angle off.
- A15 expects A to be at -90 already. Run it anywhere else and the answer is meaningless.

title: MX520 Laser calibration
body:
## What this is
Step to recalibrate Laser Tool setter after some Macro has been changed.

## When to do it
Do this when you can not get Z tool offset,G100 & G101 tool just go down and alarm up. After playing with some MACRO & I accidently changed some Macro that should NOT be change. This will reset and put everything back to normal.

## What you need
Calibration tool **M-2253-1263**.

## Steps
1. Put the calibration tool in the spindle.
2. On the **tool offset page**, enter that tool number, then its **H** (length) and
   **D** (diameter) under **Geometry**.
3. Run **O8501**.
4. **Clean all the coolant off.**
5. Run **O8502**.

O8502 can be run again if you want to be sure the coolant is really gone.

## Why step 4 matters
Coolant left on the stylus or the calibration surface sits between the ball and the metal.
The probe reads that film as part of the part, so the whole calibration comes out wrong.
Wipe it dry, not damp.

## Watch out
- Getting H or D wrong in step 2 poisons everything downstream. Check the numbers twice
  before running.
- [WHAT O8501 DOES — fill in]
- [WHAT O8502 DOES — fill in]
- [HOW TO TELL IT WORKED — is there a number to check afterward?]

title: WorkOffset Register
body:
**Read this first.** This note explains **how to work the numbers out**. It is not a list
of slot numbers for our machines.

Every control is different. The base numbers, how many offsets exist, and which axes are in
the block all change from machine to machine. Work it out for the machine in front of you
and **check it against the offset page before you write to anything**.

## What this is for
Every work offset lives in a numbered memory slot inside the control. Those slots are
called **system variables**, and they look like `#7001`.

If you know the slot number, a macro can **read** what is in an offset, or **write** a new
value into it. That is how a program sets its own work offsets instead of somebody typing
numbers into the offset page.

This note is how to work out which slot number goes with which offset.

## The layout
The extended work offsets are `G54.1 P1`, `G54.1 P2`, and so on.

Each one gets a block of **20 slots**. Inside each block the axes sit in the same order
every time:

- **+1** is X
- **+2** is Y
- **+3** is Z
- **+4** is B

So P1 starts at 7001, P2 starts 20 higher at 7021, P3 at 7041, and so on up.

## The formula
`#[20 * (n - 1) + base]`

**n** is the P number. **base** is 7001 for X, 7002 for Y, 7003 for Z, 7004 for B.

## Worked example — G54.1 P34
`X: #[20 * (34-1) + 7001] = #7661`

`Y: #[20 * (34-1) + 7002] = #7662`

`Z: #[20 * (34-1) + 7003] = #7663`

`B: #[20 * (34-1) + 7004] = #7664`

## Quick reference
- **P1** — X `#7001`, Y `#7002`, Z `#7003`, B `#7004`
- **P2** — X `#7021`, Y `#7022`, Z `#7023`, B `#7024`
- **P3** — X `#7041`, Y `#7042`, Z `#7043`, B `#7044`
- **P48** — X `#7941`, Y `#7942`, Z `#7943`, B `#7944`

Counting in twenties gets you to any of them from here.

## Going past P48
With base 7001 the numbers stop working at P48. `#7961` is **not** P49.

Add 7000 to each base and the same formula keeps going:

`#[20 * (n - 1) + 14001]`    X

`#[20 * (n - 1) + 14002]`    Y

`#[20 * (n - 1) + 14003]`    Z

`#[20 * (n - 1) + 14004]`    B

P2 comes out as `#14021`. P152 comes out as `#17021`.

For P1 through P48 both numbering schemes point at the same offset. Either works. The
14001 base is the one to use if you want a program that keeps working past P48.

## Watch out
- **Writing to one of these changes the real work offset.** Not a copy, not a scratch
  value. Get the slot number wrong and you have quietly moved a different setup's zero.
- **Check the range on your own machine.** The source for this had a control going up to
  P300. Our MX-520 probe cycles only map as far as P48, so the higher numbers may not
  exist here. Test on a spare offset first.
- Always wrap the arithmetic in square brackets: `#[20*[n-1]+7001]`. Without them the
  control reads the expression wrong.

## Correction to the original note
The last line of the source reads:

`G54.1 P3 = [20(13-1) + 7004] = #7244`

That math is right but the label is wrong. **7244 is P13, not P3.** P3 on B is
`20*(3-1) + 7004 = #7044`.

## Source
Shop reference text, author unknown. Formulas checked by hand.

title: Setting a LARGE (oversize) tool
body:
## Know first
The magazine is random-pot. After M06 the spindle tool swaps with the next tool right away,
so a tool does **not** go back to the pot it came from. The pot is the fixed thing, not the
tool.

A tool sitting in the spindle cannot be edited — its TOOL SET value is locked. Get it back
into a magazine pot first.

**LARGE** is not in the TOOL SET list at first. The control derives it from the pot layout
once the neighbors are blocked out.

## Procedure
1. Run a tool change so the tool returns to the magazine.
2. Read the pot number off the POT DETAIL panel. Do not assume it is the pot it started in.
3. **Physically pull the tools out of the pots on either side.** The pot has to be empty,
   not just marked.
4. Each neighbor pot: **[EDIT]** soft key, cursor on TOOL SET, set to **INHI.**
5. Go back to the middle pot — **LARGE** shows up on its own.

img: notes-img/pot-set-inhi.jpg | Neighbor pot 035 set to INHI. **Pot 037 on the other side was set the same way** — only one is pictured. The list still shows tool 0036 against 035; that is leftover registration, the pot itself is empty.

img: notes-img/pot-set-large.jpg | Pot 036 next to it now reads LARGE. Nobody typed that in — the control worked it out from the INHI neighbor.

img: notes-img/tool-set-types.jpg | From the manual — the TOOL SET options and how to reach them.

## Verified
Cycled tool changes about 10 minutes and the tool held its pot. INHI takes both neighbors
out of the swap pool, so the large tool has nowhere else to land.

## The tool number left behind
The pot keeps showing its old tool number in the list even after you empty it and set INHI.
In the photo, pot 035 still reads 0036 and pot 037 still reads 0030.

**Both of those tool numbers are now dead.** Call T36 or T30 and the machine alarms out,
because their pots are inhibited. So before you walk away:

- Check no program on this machine calls either tool number.
- If something does, move that tool to a free pot and update the program.
- Tell whoever is running it. An alarm mid-job at 2am over a tool number nobody mentioned
  is a bad night.

## Watch out
- HEAVY and LARGE are different. HEAVY is weight and slows the ATC arm. LARGE is diameter.
- Confirm neighbor pot numbers against the magazine or the graphical view. List order is not
  always physical order.
- TOOL SET options on this control: NORMAL, HEAVY, LARGE, INHI., PROBE, CALIB.
- Probe is tool #60 on this machine.
- Max tool diameter is commonly listed as 80 mm, or 150 mm with empty adjacent pockets.
  Check the machine's own spec before trusting that.

title: Alarm "Sub Arm not in spindle side"
body:
## When it shows up
Mostly after **air pressure drops**, or an **E-stop during a tool change**.

## Fix
1. Move the spindle back to tool change position first: `G30 X0. Y0.` — do not skip this.
2. **Reset**
3. **Setting** then **Custom** then **ATC** then **MDI**
4. **#2 open ATC door**
5. **Pot unlock**
6. **Pot Spindle side**
7. **Pot Down**
8. **Pot Lock**
9. Hit **Program**, type **M6**, then **Cycle Start**.

title: Spline in MCAM
body:
Do **not** use a spline to chain a toolpath.

Project 3D toolpaths take forever to regenerate off a spline.

Draw a **line or arc** instead and chain to that.

title: G131 / HON — speed vs precision
body:
## What it does
One line in the program tells the machine how hard to trade **speed** against **precision**.
Put it near the top, before the cutting.

## Touch panel machines — pick by job type
Low number = faster. High number = tighter. Middle = balanced, leaning tight.

- **G131P1-3** — prismatic. 2-axis and helical work.
- **G131M1-3** — multi-surface. 3-axis work.
- **G131F1-3** — 5-axis simultaneous. Works for 4-axis too.
- **G131D1** — drilling and tapping. Lets the machine accelerate harder, since canned cycles
  are positional and have no profile to hold.

For P, M and F: **1** = speed and smoothness, **3** = precision, **2** = a decent balance
still leaning toward precision.

## Older R-level way
`HONR0-10` or `G131R0-10`. **0** = speed, **10** = precision, in between is a blend.

## Watch out
- HON still works, but it needs the right variable and value or it does nothing.
- A program containing HON has to be **loaded in** from USB, Compact Flash or RS-232. Typing
  it at the control will not work.
- Pick by what the job needs: roughing and drilling want speed, finish surfaces want
  precision.

## Source
Selway Machine Tool applications bulletin, 2/23/2021 — "Matsuura G131/HON Explained, New
Matsuura Machines".
